title: Unto the mountains (Psalm 121)
hook: "He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one thirty, a cry from the depths. Your line was out of the depths. Did you say one honest word from a low place? Today, we look up. Day three hundred twenty-five.

Think about the last time you were watching over someone through the night. A sick child. A parent in the hospital. A friend on the couch after a terrible day. You try to stay awake, and sooner or later your head drops. Nobody can keep watch forever. We all sleep. That's exactly the thought behind one of the most beloved psalms, often said for travelers, for newborns, and for anyone who needs protecting. It starts with a person looking at the mountains. Today: Psalm one twenty-one.
screen: `WATCHING OVER SOMEONE AT NIGHT.` → `YOUR HEAD DROPS.` → `NOBODY CAN KEEP WATCH FOREVER.`

segments.voice: It's another Song of Ascents, one of the pilgrim songs. Picture a traveler on the road to Jerusalem, looking up at the hills ahead. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: from whence shall my help come?" The mountains are beautiful, and they're also where danger hides on a long journey. And the answer comes straight back: my help comes from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth. Not from the mountains. From the One who made them. Then the psalm's great promise: "Behold, He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep." The Hebrew word is shomer: a keeper, a guard, a watchman. It's the word for someone on the night shift, the one who keeps watch while others rest. In just eight verses, forms of that word appear six times. The Lord is your keeper. He'll keep you from all evil. He'll keep your going out and your coming in, from now and forever. The sun won't strike you by day, nor the moon by night. That's why Jews say this psalm for protection: before a journey, for a woman giving birth, at a sickbed. It's often printed on cards hung near a newborn's crib. And Hasidic teachers found a hidden reading in the opening question. From where, me-ayin, can also be heard as from ayin, from nothingness. Help comes out of the moment when you admit you have nothing left. Someone is keeping watch when you can't.
screen: `EYES LIFTED TO THE MOUNTAINS.` · `HELP FROM THE MAKER OF HEAVEN.` · `SHOMER: THE KEEPER.` · `ME-AYIN: FROM NOTHING.` · then, large: `HE DOESN'T SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a hill or the horizon. If you can see one from where you are, a hill, a skyline, the edge of the sky, look at it. If not, close your eyes and picture a range of mountains far off. Settle, and breathe. Lift your eyes, literally. Notice how different it feels to look up and out instead of down. Ask the psalm's question quietly: where will my help come from? Think of the people you're watching over. Picture them kept, even while you sleep. If you pray, you can say the psalm's promise. The bell holds the time.
Unto the mountains. Psalm one twenty-one: I lift my eyes and ask where help will come from, and the answer is a keeper who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
Your line: he doesn't sleep. Tonight, when you put down the worries you're keeping watch over, let someone else hold the night shift. Day three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Many Jews recite Psalm 121 before travel, at a sickbed and for protection in childbirth; it is often printed on cards or plaques placed near a newborn, and it is part of the Shabbat afternoon psalms in some communities.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty psalm about the hills.
what it means: a promise that someone keeps watch when you can't, on every journey.

what a scholar hears: the heading is shir la-ma'alot, slightly different from the other Songs of Ascents, the root sh-m-r runs through the psalm, and Hasidic readers hear me-ayin as 'from nothingness'.
